utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We have to deal with a few procedural matters first. I, first of all, would like to go into private session, but it will not take any more than half a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. There were some other procedural issues to be raised. One would be raised either at the end or the beginning. I think it's checked on the transcript what has been said by Mr. Tieger, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been checked on the transcript. There was no specification whether it would be at the beginning or at the end, so therefore both parties were right or wrong. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm sorry, I was under the impression that we were going to take it up at the end of the session, but I'm happy to address it now. In relation to the cross-examination of Mr. Davidovic, Your Honours will recall at the time I expressed some concern about some of the questions that were being put to the witness, as I -- I was uncertain of what the -- the good-faith basis was for some of those very serious allegations that were being made against Mr. Davidovic, calling him a criminal and a liar. At the time I objected and questioned the basis. I don't have any objection or quarrel with the Defence statement, then, when counsel has reasonable grounds to believe that it has information that impeaches an adverse witness. Then counsel should ask questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps remind us, Mr. Hannis, what day exactly it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was -- most of the questions I'm talking about, Your Honour, were on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially the -- the questions in cross- examination on -- I think on being robbed of --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That was the 27th of June, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, in particular the questions -- I've given the Court a chart, I believe; I don't know if you have that. I sent an e-mail to your legal officer which contained a copy. I have hard copies I can hand up now, Your Honour, that has specific references. Some of the questions were on the 13th, but the ones -- most in particular were on the 27th. As I said, I don't have -- I don't have a quarrel with the proposition that when there's a reasonable ground, that there is impeaching information, then counsel should ask those questions. But it's our position, Your Honour, that there's also an obligation on counsel's part to exercise caution in making such serious allegation against a witness. And the fact that we've got a sort of judicial immunity as advocates should not be a licence to slander or engage in character assassination. Reasonable grounds to believe should be an objective standard, not merely a subjective one. We have evidence to show that several Defence counsel questions are not supported and were not supported at the time that they were asked by objective reasonable grounds. I've prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least, Mr. Hannis, we do not know about such support. Isn't that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we still have to hear the Defence on the matter as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. As I've said, I've set out some of these grounds on the chart. One of the questions referred to the specific question about Mr. Davidovic currently having three criminal complaints against him. We were furnished some documents that related to those questions, and as I've set forth in the chart, Your Honour, it appears to me that it does not support that implication that there were criminal complaints against him. I think in the context of the question, it would reasonably be understood as saying that there were actually criminal proceedings, not the mere fact that a private individual had written a letter to the Prosecutor complaining about somebody's conduct. But one of the most troubling examples relates to Defence counsel's rigorous assertions that Mr. Davidovic exploited Bosniaks during the war by taking property from them. In particular, I refer to the June 27th transcript citation at page 15.225, beginning at line 17. The question was, "Now, Mr. Davidovic, you seized all the furnishings and equipment from the dental office of Dr. Edina Alabaci Hujdurovic in Bijeljina, didn't you? In fact, Mr. Davidovic, after seeing you on Television Bosnia giving your evidence two weeks ago, Dr. Hujdurovic, Dr. Edina Alabaci Hujdurovic spoke out on local TV about you doing just that." Your Honour, I hope that you have copies of the affidavits from her, her husband, and her office assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have received the affidavits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which do speak to this issue. And I believe from what they say, it appears there was no basis. Most troubling about that is -- is the fact that her husband indicates the morning of June the 27th he received two phone calls; one from an individual in Belgrade, whose phone number we have - but I don't have that number in front of me, but I will furnish that to Defence counsel and the Court. I think I've already sent it by e-mail to Defence counsel - in which the husband was asked if it was true that his wife had appeared on local TV and said that thing. He told the caller that that was not true. And half an hour later he received a second phone call from a telephone number which we have now checked, and our information indicates that is a phone number that is associated with the case manager for the Krajisnik Defence counsel. And he spoke to that individual, who he said gave the name that sounded something like Radojcic, who asked if it was true that his wife had gone on TV and said those things. He again told that person no, that she had not said that, that her property had never been seized by Mr. Davidovic nor by anyone, and that they did not want their name used or spoken of in court proceedings. Your Honour, for many months the Prosecution has heard Defence counsel put down markers for us where it was felt that our conduct or manner of proceeding was improper or out of line. Today I want to put down a marker on behalf of Mr. Davidovic and any future witnesses that allegations of criminal conduct and -- and perjury should not be so vigorously asserted without an objective good-faith basis. We leave it to Your Honours to examine the record and our submissions on this matter. We believe that what appears so far raises sufficient ground for further inquiry. Now, that may be a matter between the Bench and the Defence team outside our presence, as it may involve attorney-client communications. I would merely ask that if your view -- if your review satisfies you that -- that due diligence was not exercised in this manner, and as you yourself, Judge Orie, said at page 15.309, "It would be of concern to the Chamber whenever a witness would be uncomfortable for any reason that should not make him uncomfortable." We believe there was and is cause for concern here, and if you so find, then steps should be taken to prevent similar results in the future. Now, while we cannot undo certain harm that may have been done, an apology to the witness might be appropriate and would go some way, Your Honour, toward helping him explain to his five-year-old grandson why he was being called a criminal. Now, that's all I have to submit on this matter at this time, Your Honour. Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Ms. Loukas, I can imagine that you would like to take some time before responding, but I also can imagine that, since, I take it, part of the information Mr. Hannis provides to the Chamber is already known to you, that you would respond immediately. I leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, firstly, of course, I indicated on the day that Mr. Hannis first raised this, and Your Honour will recall that I -- I made very clear that, Your Honour, I did have a reasonable basis for putting the questions, firstly, and I also made the -- the point, Your Honours, that as an advocate I have a duty to put the questions, and if information is supplied and I don't put the questions, then Mr. Krajisnik has a basis to complain about my conduct. There's a very important balance here to be maintained by an advocate. And I also made the point at the time, Your Honour, that these matters were raised on the 27th of June that, it is my obligation to put questions where there is information of this nature, and it's an obligation that an advocate should never shirk from, regardless of how unpopular it might make one, with the Prosecution or the witness or whoever. Now, Your Honour, I take it, as I had a discussion with Mr. Hannis earlier today, as -- as I understood it, my conduct was not under attack. If it is, I would like to know that very specifically, Your Honour, because then I have to take a different course in addressing these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any reason to believe that Ms. Loukas wasn't told that the dentist appeared on television and made that statement, but my concern is about who -- who told her that based on the information that the Krajisnik Defence team was provided in those two phone calls by her husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would like to say something about this. The -- the principles are -- are really very clear. It is counsel's responsibility to make a conscientious professional assessment of the reliability of instructions and information given before putting matters to the witness, and Ms. Loukas has assured the Court that she has done that, Your Honour. And so far as that element of the matter is concerned, then in my submission, that is simply -- and certainly as far as I'm concerned, because this is one of those areas where as lead counsel I am entitled to assert my personal position, as opposed to simply a matter of submission. So that's an end of that particular point. And it appears, in any case, it's an end of that particular point, as far as the Prosecution is concerned because that's what Mr. Hannis has just confirmed. Your Honour, what this cannot become, then, while acknowledging up to a point legitimate concerns by the Prosecution that information which reaches counsel should at all times be conscientiously assessed, what it can't become, then, is some sort of fishing exercise by the Prosecution then to start investigating beyond the specific information -- or the assurance of counsel, to go behind that to then investigate what the sources of information are. If on this occasion - and I say "if" because it's part of the responsibility of counsel not just conscientiously to assess the position in advance but, of course, in the light of any such concerns, as are expressed by the Prosecution here, retrospectively to assess that information, so far as it might cast any light for the future. Not to conduct some ex post facto inquiry into the specific information in relation to this particular matter, but just to absorb any lessons or information and absorb any information that we have as to reliability -- reliability or unreliability of sources for future reference. And that's part of the learning process, and that's a matter which counsel would take account of in the future. But it is not the appropriate course, in our submission, to start exploring now, in light of Ms. Loukas's assurance and the Prosecution's acceptance of her professional position to start going into the facts here. We note the concerns. We bear those concerns in mind for the future. We will at all times conscientiously exercise our professional judgement in relation to such matters having regard to all the information at our disposal, and that is what we undertake to the Court to do for the future. But this should not become any sort of mini trial or investigation in relation to these particular matters which were put to the witness. They were put by Ms. Loukas in good faith. We note what's been said. We will continue to do our job conscientiously for the future, and we strongly submit that that is, in relation to this particular matter, an end to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just -- I haven't got the affidavits in front of me. Again, I remember that the telephone calls were made relatively early in the morning of what is the 17th or the 27th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The 27th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 27th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have an extra copy, if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- well, I think I have it relatively clear on my mind. I remember the second phone call was at 9.15, if I'm ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first call was about 8.30 or 8.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the second call half an hour after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just after 9.00. And at what time - because I did not check that of course - at what time approximately were the questions put to the witness about seizing all the furnishings and equipment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was a morning or an afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I recall, the 27th was an afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An afternoon session. Yes, that's just what I was trying to reconstruct. The Chamber will consider the matter, Mr. Stewart, but the parties have responsibilities, one to the other: Parties have responsibilities towards witnesses, their own witnesses, witnesses of the other party. The parties have responsibilities towards the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber itself also has responsibilities towards the witnesses, whether Defence or Prosecution witnesses. One of the matters the Chamber will consider whether it needs further attention is whether it needs some further analysis, assuming - and that's perhaps the first thing, then, to be verified - that such telephone calls have taken place in the early morning of the 27th of June. That perhaps needs some verification, as well. And it needs further analysis whether, and if so, Witness Davidovic was treated in an unfair way - that's one - and, second, if he was, what caused this to happen; and, third, what, if the questions are answered in affirmative, what should be done in order to avoid this to happen again. Whether that would be something the Chamber should do, whether it would be something the parties should do, that's all open. But the matter, whether we will give further attention to it, we'll consider that, and we'll let the parties know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the -- just two things. A matter of information, Your Honour, so as to avoid any misunderstanding at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do confirm that the telephone call from the mobile telephone number belonging to my case manager, Mr. Karganovic, was a call made by him. And we do not in the least bit shrink from that. We feel -- I feel it is correct that the Trial Chamber should know that absolutely unequivocally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The second thing I will say is this, Your Honour: And that while maintaining our position, it really ought not -- such matters ought not to be the subject of some retrospective mini trial. Of course, if as a result of discussions between the Prosecution and the Defence in this case -- after all, it might be the other way round on future occasions -- if as a result of discussions between the parties, we on our side in this case were satisfied that although conscientiously put at the time to the witness, in fact, on further examination it is clear that the allegation conscientiously in good faith put to the witness is, in fact, not correct. Your Honour, we would simply withdraw it, and we would publicly withdraw it. That would be the proper course to take. However, we suggest that one should be careful not to open the matter up so that allegations put to witnesses in good faith then became even remotely routinely the matter of some -- some further inquiry. Because there is a point, where we all, I hope, show proper concern for witnesses -- there is a point at which such matters -- I'm not saying anything about all the allegations here -- are, with respect, part of the rough and tumble of coming to give evidence in court. But, Your Honour, certainly in relation to anything of any significance at all where we are satisfied that though put in good faith it did not, in fact, well-founded, Your Honour, that we would, of course, unequivocally withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I, of course, place it on the record, Your Honour, precisely in those terms as expressed by lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider the matter to see whether, and if so, what further activities should be deployed by the Chamber. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing further from me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. HANNIS: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I should say thank you, Mr. Hannis. There was that misunderstanding as to whether it was at the beginning or end of the day. It's most helpful to me that he's agreed to come down and deal with it now, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He's living closer by.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's true. But nevertheless, it's still appreciated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Since I am here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- no, very briefly, Your Honour, on a entirely different but nevertheless important issue, I -- this is not, now, to be some elaborate lengthy submission, Your Honour, but just to make the position clear, in a nutshell, I said that I would consider and discuss over the weekend the position generally that we are in particularly relating to Mr. Krajisnik's announcement some weeks ago now that he wished to represent himself and the consequential negotiations which have been going on in some sorts of directions since. Your Honour, the position, as we can assess it on the Defence side, is this: On one particular issue, negotiations between Mr. Krajisnik and the Registry do appear to have reached an impasse. I have been to see Mr. Krajisnik again this morning. That is frankly my assessment. We have explored that; that does appear to be everybody's assessment among those concerned. Your Honour, I have in a sense, although it's unhappy to express it in exactly those terms -- I do in a sense have my -- or Mr. Krajisnik and I have our own negotiations. There is, of course, always an area in which there's something along the lines of negotiation between client and counsel on any difficult case, as I'm sure everybody would agree this one is. On one point in particular - it may be two points. It doesn't matter how one analyses it - but on one particular important point, Mr. Krajisnik and I are also at an impasse. There is perhaps another point where we've been at an impasse for so long that we've probably each of us seized to notice it's an impasse any more, but it nevertheless is. But, Your Honour, one of the matters which I have explored with Mr. Krajisnik is what appears to be in some sense the logical consequence or at least something closely connected logically with the Trial Chamber's decision so far to allow Mr. Krajisnik to cross-examine witnesses in addition to cross-examination conducted by counsel. Now, not surprisingly, Mr. Krajisnik infers that the Trial Chamber's position in relation to cross-examination of witnesses would apply equally to examination of Defence witnesses, so that he would have the right to supplement examination of Defence witnesses when counsel has finished that examination. But further connected with that and logically as part of the same principle, the question which has been discussed between Mr. Krajisnik and me - and we would at least suggest it's an intelligent question for us to have discussed - is, who has the right to decide which witnesses to call in the first place? Because if you don't call a witness, you can't question the witness, and logically those two matters are very difficult to distinguish in principle. And since the Trial Chamber's decision has created and continues to create enormous difficulties between Mr. Krajisnik and me in relation -- or between counsel and Mr. Krajisnik, but I must say I do feel slightly at the sharp end as far as counsel is concerned on -- on this issue. I don't mind. I work at the sharp end as lead counsel. But we -- we have reached or failed to reach, if you like -- we have come to enormous difficulties between the two of us in relation to that matter. We correspondingly are now facing enormous difficulties in resolving that issue. And I simply today put on the table, as one among a number of matters which are still going to require careful and thorough and mature exploration and consideration, what are the implications of the position adopted at the moment if I and -- sorry, whatever co-counsel is with me continue as assigned counsel for Mr. Krajisnik? What are the implications for our conduct of the case, which is what we are supposed to have, in relation to such matters as who decides which witnesses to call, who decides which witnesses not to call, who decides which documents to put before the Trial Chamber, who decides which documents not to put before the Trial Chamber. As I put the questions, Your Honours, I hope it can be seen that the answers are not absolutely straightforward, and the practical implications are extremely difficult. Your Honour, as a practical matter right now it leads to this: It's a scheduling matter, as well, Your Honour. We have Mr. Brown coming to give evidence now. And on the projected time estimate from Mr. Harmon and on our assessment of time, Mr. Brown is, for practical purposes, going to take up today, Tuesday, and Wednesday. It looks as if his evidence is going to fit those days allowed. It's not going to leave anything to spare. On the other hand, the earnest hope all around is that he will be finished by close of play on Wednesday because Thursday and Friday are virtually sacrosanct non-sitting for the reasons the Trial Chamber has indicated, and then we have witnesses that I won't name because, again, I can never remember exactly which of them are protected and which aren't. But we have witnesses coming along then Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, spilling quite possibly into Thursday, and then another witness on Friday when the whole Prosecution case is supposed to finish and, indeed, the recess starts. So, Your Honour, I simply raise the practical question, since it's clear that if we don't achieve the unexpected breakthrough of all these negotiations falling into place and everything being resolved, which I have to conscientiously inform the Trial Chamber seems a remote possibility at the moment, then some substantial time is going to be required to resolve these issues because, again, I'm quite confident that the Trial Chamber, as everybody else, feels that everybody has to know where they are, at least some useful time before we all break up on the 22nd of -- of July to do whatever we have to do next. If we're lucky enough to go on holiday, we're lucky enough, and if we're unlucky, we don't. But whatever happens, we're not sitting after that date. So, Your Honour, that's the practical position, and I think I've felt it was only fair to give the Trial Chamber that indication of where the Defence sees that we are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll again carefully read your words, Mr. Stewart, and we'll consider the present situation and see whether, apart from being informed, the Chamber will respond to those observations or just -- we'll wait and see how matters develop. Meanwhile, just for the completeness of the transcript, Mr. Krajisnik, you have sent a letter to the Judges in which you explain more or less how you evaluate the talks you had with the representative of the Registry. It took us some time to have this letter translated. Are there any changes since you wrote us that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had a talk with the Chamber -- or rather, with the Registry, and I think that we have exhausted all the possibilities. These talks have thus been brought to a conclusion. What Mr. Stewart has said are talks between the two of us, and new problems keep arising. I thought that we could bring this to an end and simply have done with all the problems. It's not that I don't feel that Mr. Stewart is right, but I feel that a client and his counsel have to cooperate closely. I don't think that I have to direct Mr. Stewart's actions, but I do feel I have to be an active participant and not just an observer. That's what I spoke about with Mr. Stewart this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was mainly asking whether any new developments in your conversations with the Registry took place, but I do understand that you have not reached a final agreement with the Registry, so therefore the situation is not anything different from what you wrote to us. Thank you very much, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, could I just say one more thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just a small -- well, it's not a small thing, Your Honour. We have Miss Tara Powers as a member of the Defence team in court. It's the first time she's been in court on this case, so I wanted to introduce her to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution. She's actually -- unhappily, as often happens, she's leaving us very soon, which we regret. We've been unable to persuade to her say. But she's here today, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Powers, welcome in court. I think no one has ever been introduced, first of all, with the words "it's not a small thing." But welcome, and I hope your contribution to the Defence will be a fruitful one. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness will be Mr. Ewan Brown, who will testify as an expert in respect of military matters relating to the 1 Krajina Corps. For your information, Your Honour, I have distributed four binders to the Chamber with exhibits that will be referred to by Mr. Brown. I would ask the Court's permission to permit Mr. Brown to keep at his side portions of the exhibits that are contained in the binders that I have submitted to you, specifically his own expert report, the errata sheet, the report on the army, and the transcript from the 16th Session. Those are long items, lengthy items in the report, and Mr. Brown has made some marks on them to indicate and quickly find passages that he would like to refer to. And if the Court has -- and the counsel has no objection, then I would ask that those be permitted -- Mr. Brown be permitted to keep those by his side, rather than have wholly blank documents -- wholly unmarked documents in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Defence has no objections, the Chamber has no objections either.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can indicate, Your Honour, I have no objections, firstly. I would also raise two other matters, if I may, at this juncture, and that is: Firstly, I'm in receipt of the errata sheet. That was, in fact, only e-mailed yesterday afternoon, on Sunday, and, of course, it's a report that is about to celebrate its third anniversary. So I think it's - - I must place on the record that it's most unfortunate that this errata sheet -- and the -- was delivered to the Defence at such a -- a late stage, firstly. I've had discussions with Mr. Harmon about it, and a significant proportion appear to be in the nature of typos and what have you. But a number of the entries actually arise from the cross-examination of Mr. Brown in the trial of Mr. Brdjanin, and they're significant matters. And in those circumstances, it's -- it's surprising that it took so long to correct the report. That's the first matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honour, I can indicate that the Defence have -- have a military expert that we would be wishing to have present in court during the evidence in chief and cross-examination. I can indicate that a similar application was made in respect of a Defence military expert in the Brdjanin trial that was accepted, and there's quite clearly a precedent for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I make that application, Your Honour. I place that on the record, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objection, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, as long as the expert will be identified for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, the request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I can indicate that it is a Mr. Mirko Trivic, spelled T-r-i-v-i-c. He's a retired army officer, and his rank is colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just for the record, can we have the corps; did he serve with the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I actually don't have the specific corps noted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It would be helpful if we could have that information, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that your concern might be, Mr. Harmon, that experts who were perhaps involved in whatever activity that would be covered by the indictment would not be applauded by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Or other indictments, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or other indictments. At the same time, Mr. Harmon, it might not, looking at the number of indictments related to all parties, it might not be easy to find a military expert who is totally out of that, but let's first see what the facts are.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can indicate he gave evidence to the Prosecution in Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, then, that in the testimony in the Brdjanin case he said something about his career. Is that ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I also indicate, Your Honour, of course, that the -- and I will place this on the record, as well: The Defence has again, as has been the case throughout the conduct of this case, had not nearly enough time to prepare appropriately for a witness of this significance. We have at the last moment been able to find a Defence expert. He flew in on Saturday; I spent all day Sunday with him. Your Honour, I -- I can indicate that there's a real question as to whether we will, in fact, be in a position to commence the cross- examination straight after the end of the evidence in chief. Yet again, as we have been throughout, in terms of the inadequate time we have been given as the Defence in preparation of this case, had to do too much with too little for too long, and that, yet again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- is the case in relation to a witness of this significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I shouldn't have said Brdjanin. It was Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blagojevic. I take it that you don't have that information by heart. Otherwise, I think you would tell Mr. Harmon, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour. He gave evidence for the Prosecution in the case of Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic, and -- and there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what he said about where he was active in the period 1992 up until --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I -- I understand, Your Honour, that it may, in fact, have been the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just need to confirm that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Mr. Harmon, let's -- at this moment, I take it that you would like further to inquire into the matter before you further respond to the question. We have at this moment a very practical matter, that is, whether we allow him to sit next to the Defence and hear it from this side of the glass wall or whether we'd -- we would not allow him to do that when I expect him to hear everything from the other side of the glass wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be inappropriate to bring him in at this point in any event because I raised with the court officer certain sensitivities in which I will be required to go into private session briefly during the examination of Mr. Brown in respect of his background. So I -- it would be inappropriate to have the witness in the courtroom during that particular portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from the private session, you take no strict position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At this point I take no strict position. I'm making an inquiry at this very moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- to find out about Mr. Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's, then, part of the -- Ms. Loukas, part of the testimony which would be given in private session Mr. Harmon objects against your expert being present during that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, Mr. Harmon raised this issue just prior to our coming into court today, and it's just a question of a portion of the curriculum vitae. It's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Are we going to start with that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I suggest that the witness will be called, that he'll give his solemn declaration, that we start with the testimony in private session, and that on from that moment, Ms. Loukas, that your expert, with all reservations Mr. Harmon has made as to whether he will object or not, will be -- can sit next to you at the Defence bench for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can start in public session, and then we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I mean, the testimony, and then, of course, the solemn declaration should first of all be given in public session. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, since we speak the same language, I'm going to ask you to pause between question and answer because of the difficulties the language booth has in interpreting as quickly as we speak. So if you would remember to pause between question and answer, it would be appreciated. Also, Mr. Brown, I've informed the Court that you have in front of you your report, the errata sheet, the army analysis, and the transcript of the 16th Session where you have marked certain portions you may wish to refer to. And let me inform you there's no objection to your having those before you. Mr. Brown, let me -- let me now begin, and I'd like you to affirm the following. First of all, could you state your complete name and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: My name is Ewan McGreggor Brown, that's B-r-o-w-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, were you born on the 15th of May, 1964? Are you a British citizen? Are you currently employed as an investigator at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, and have you been so employed since 2005? Do you hold a bachelors degree in history from the University of East Anglia, a masters degree from criminology from the University of Leicester, and did you attend the Royal Military Academy in Sandhurst, where thereafter you were commissioned as an officer in the British army?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, if we can go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Ms. Loukas, this is the moment that your -- the expert you're consulting at this moment - let's put it that way - could sit next to you, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'll just see that procedures can be put into place in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, now, you were a military analyst in the Office of the Prosecutor from 1998 to 2004; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber the role of a military analyst in the Office of the Prosecutor, what functions you performed.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: There is a small, dedicated team within the Office of the Prosecutor formed predominantly from ex-military officers and military personnel; invariably, ex-intelligence officers are people who work in military analysis. It is their job to provide analytical support to the investigative teams or to the senior trial attorneys. That work invariably means assisting in interpreting material, reviewing documentation, military documentation, and generally giving advice in relation to military issues, should they require it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in the course of performing your duties in the Office of the Prosecutor, did you work with materials from the JNA and from the Bosnian Serb Army, the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you work with those materials over the course of six years?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I did, amongst other things, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could tender Mr. Brown's resume, which is found in tab 1 of the first binder that you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you want to tender that under seal, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And let's just see. When we go to numbering, I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we used to give one number to the whole bunch of it and then say exhibit so-and-so, tab so-and-so. But we could perhaps start with the resume and give that a number under seal, then give the report one number and all the tabs a similar number, but then with the addition tab so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The curriculum vitae will be Prosecution Exhibit P890, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you prepared a -- an expert report entitled "Military developments in the Bosanska Krajina 1992." It is dated the 21st of July, 2002. Who asked you to prepare that report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Ms. Jo Korner, who was a senior trial attorney working in the Office of the Prosecutor at the time, asked me to compile the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What directions were you given in respect of preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner gave me something of -- some relatively general guidance that she wanted a report produced based on -- predominantly based on documentation about the military activities in the Krajina, but it was very relatively general and was not necessarily detailed or specific. But she wanted a report compiled based on material that we had, reviewing that material on military activities and developments in the Krajina in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you mainly use documentary material in preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think I -- apart from some videos, I think it's exclusively documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber what types of documents you examined.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I prodominantly used military documentation. A large section of that had been obtained as a result of search -- search and seizure tasks that the Office of the Prosecutor had conducted. Most of the documents or a significant percentage of the documents are military documents. I also utilised some police documents. Again, many of these had been taken as a result of search operations. I utilised some political documents, which I predominantly utilised if they related to Defence or military issues. I also used a small number, I think, of open-source documents, media articles and the likes, and some videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You say certain documents were the result of searches and seizures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say that you utilised documents that had been seized by the Office of the Prosecutor pursuant to searches, did that include the documentation from the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. There was a search and seizure operation which had happened actually before I had arrived to the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps, and a significant section of that archive was -- was taken back here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, in preparing this report, who selected the documents that formed the basis of this report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many documents did you use in the preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm not actually sure of the exact number, but I know -- I think there was around 900 footnotes. Not the footnotes -- not every footnote relates to an individual document. There's multiple references. I think there's probably around about 600 or so individual documents, maybe a little less, but around that number, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was your objective in preparing this report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, my objective was to -- to look at the documentation and where I could, give an analysis of, as the title suggests, military developments in Bosanska Krajina in 1992 as best as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is an index in this report. In respect of that index, can you tell us whose decision it was to organise this report in this manner?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It was mine and mine alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what limitations, if any, does this report have, in your view?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. There are limitations to this report, and I think I even stressed some of those in the introduction. There's a limitation in relation to time. It only deals predominantly with 1992; it does refer a little bit to 1991. Some documents, I believe, also reference 1993, but it's predominantly about 1992. So there's a limitation in relation to that. It's limited in relation to the source of the material. It's -- it's documentary based. It's not relating to witness testimony or any sources of information. So that is a limitation to some degree. It's limited, of course, in relation to my ability to search and -- and conduct analysis on -- on many, many documents that we do have in the Office of the Prosecutor. I couldn't clearly footnote every single issue. I couldn't put in every reference necessarily that -- of documentation there. But there is a natural limitation in that respect. And these -- these, I think, are some of the references -- some of the limitations that I do have. And it does deal -- maybe another one is that it does deal to some extent very heavily with military issues. It's not about predominantly a lot of other -- the other issues that were on there at the time. So these are some of the limitations to -- of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, does Your Honour wish that at the end of the examination that I tender the binders in toto, or as we go through the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just had a brief discussion with Madam Registrar. We would like you to tender the documents. It gets -- I did say otherwise, but will get a separate number. And then a number will be assigned to -- a general number will be assigned to all the exhibits attached to the report. So I'd like you to tender the report, first of all, and then we'll see what documents you will use -- what documents you will present to the witness. And, of course, the Chamber, it would not surprise you, has similar concerns, as expressed before, with large numbers of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, then I would tender the report of Mr. Brown at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, that would be what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report will be Prosecution Exhibit P891, and the errata sheet, P891A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And could we already assign a general number for the related exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The general number for the related exhibits will be Prosecution Exhibit P892.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, what I would like to do before I get into the examination of Mr. Brown on the binders, I would be surprised if Your Honours recall, but on the 13th of February, 2004 there was an issue that was raised in respect of the testimony of Mr. Keronjic specifically, in aren't of a diary of Petar Jankovic, and there was an inquiry as to who Nikola Dencic was. And there is a reference in the diary -- Your Honour asked -- Your Honour Judge Orie asked the question about who was the godfather, and I undertook to come back to you at some point in time with the answer, and Mr. Brown is now in a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- to give you that answer. Again, I refer to the transcript of the 13th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brown, without belabouring the point, can you identify Nikola Dencic and what his role was in the JNA and later in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I believe that Nikola Dencic was a JNA officer serving in the JNA 17th Corps - the JNA 17th Corps was based in Tuzla - and he was a staff officer working that -- in that corps. He later became, I believe for a very short space of time, the first commander of the VRS East Bosnia Corps, which was headquartered in Bijeljina. I don't believe he stayed in that position for too long, but he was a JNA officer, and he was in the VRS for a short space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now we'll move to the testimony. And, Mr. Brown, in your expert report between pages 12 and 20 there is -- you referred to the JNA, and I'd like to have you address certain aspects in respect of the JNA. Are you familiar, Mr. Brown, with a concept of the All People's Army?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All People's Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court briefly what that concept was.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, briefly, All People's Defence was a means by which Yugoslavia could mobilise many aspects in the defence of the state, and the JNA was a significant component of that. And the JNA was a multi- -- made to be a multi- ethnic, multinational federal body engaged in the defence of the Yugoslav territory. And All People's Defence was a doctrine in which state and its components would be mobilised in a time of crisis in order to defend the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention, Mr. Brown, on how the JNA evolved from being a -- an army that was multi-effect and defended the different ethnic groups within the former Yugoslavia to becoming one that defended exclusively the Serb interest. And if I can direct your attention first to paragraph 1.3 of your report in which you say, and I quote, "In relation to the first aspect in particular, elements within the JNA were already aware of the problems of ethnic and party divisions in early 1992, and some evidence indicated that the JNA believed that all national parties and groups were contributing to the volatility." Why did that concern the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I -- first of all, there was the war in Croatia, which had -- there had been a negotiation by the end of 1991, but that clearly had a significant impact on -- on them. They were engaged there, and clearly ethnic tensions and ethnic divisions there had caused significant problems. But maybe more widely, I think, because ethnic divisions threatened Yugoslavia and the JNA, being a Yugoslavian or federal institution, probably realised that this was a -- was a threat to -- to Yugoslavia and a threat to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What -- in respect of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what policies did the JNA adopt as time evolved?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think I've articulated it in the report as something of a twin- track policy. I think in the early part of 1992, as forces were being withdrawn from Croatia into Bosnia, the JNA did have some references and -- and there were documentary evidence -- or there is documentary evidence that they tried to reduce ethnic tensions in a way, presumably to try and keep what was -- as much of Yugoslavia together as possible. But it's clear, also, that documentary evidence, especially by the spring of 1992, would seem to indicate that they themselves were aligning themselves with the SDS or the Bosnian Serbs, and that there is evidence that -- that they were converging and that there is also evidence that weapons were being distributed from the JNA to the Bosnian Serbs. So I think there is evidence of -- of a twin track of initially trying to diffuse ethnic tensions because they realised the ethnic tensions were likely to endanger what was left of Yugoslavia, but as the situation deteriorated, they aligned themselves very much with the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to turn to tab 4 in the binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't know if the witness has a copy of the binders in front of him, but if he could be provided with one. I'd like the first binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if you could turn to tab 4.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, this has a previous exhibit number, and I'm prepared to read off the previous exhibit numbers, if Your Honour would like, in respect of each exhibit where there is an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you present it to the witness and just mention the number. That would, for those who have to read the transcript at a later stage, be very convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P51 and P51.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if I can direct your attention to the exhibit in tab 4. This is a document classified as a military secret, and it is the conclusions based on an assessment of the situation in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, area of responsibility of the 2nd Military District. This document is dated March of 1992, and at the end of the document, it bears the signature of Milutin Kukanjac, Commander General. Can you, first of all, identify who General Kukanjac and what role he had in the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: General Kukanjac was the commander of the 2nd Military District. The 2nd Military District covered, to all intents and purposes, Bosnia- Herzegovina. It covered a little bit of Croatia, as well, but to all intents and purposes, it covered Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, have you had an opportunity to review -- you've reviewed this document. I know that. So let me ask you: In respect of this document, does this document, Mr. Brown, reflect a change in the attitude of the JNA from being neutral to being one that reflects a pro-Serb stance?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think there are a number of areas in this document that would seem to highlight that. If I take you to page 3, where they discuss the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in particular page 3 on where -- where it's highlighted "4" halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, before we get to point 4, can I direct your attention to point 2 of that document, where it says, "The Serbian people has opted for Yugoslavia." And in point 1 and point 3, it also discusses the positions, the respective positions of the SDA and the HDZ, the two political parties of the non-Serbs, and it indicates that the Serb party had opted for Yugoslavia. What's the significance of that in this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think this is another example of where I see this convergence, that clearly the JNA would have opted for Yugoslavia also and that the Serbian people have opted for Yugoslavia, and so there is this convergence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if you could give us your comments on point 4, please, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Point 4 discusses a meeting that clearly had happened with Jose Cutilheiro, where he seemed to want to hear, according to this document at least, the truest possible version, presumably the truest possible version of what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And Kukanjac writes here, "The minister was briefed in great detail about the background to the events, the real goals of the leaders of the nationalist parties and the direction where this was heading. The position taken by the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the reasons why it is justified were particularly stressed." Again, this would seem to indicate this convergence by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page in the document, on page 4. It's subpart C. And I would like to direct your attention to a sentence that appears in the middle of that paragraph. It says, "This is quite normal because the Serbian people is in all fairness under threat here yet again, and accordingly we are protecting the interests of the people." When the reference is "the Serbian people are under threat yet again," do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It's not exactly clear whether he meant over a protracted period of time or whether he was referring, say, to Croatia, as what had happened in late 1991. But it's clear that, again, I would argue that this is a statement that would seem to align certainly Kukanjac and the 2nd Military District and the JNA with -- with the Serbs. And in this case, he makes mention of the SDS leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you go -- let me pause. Mr. Brown, could you go to the end of paragraph C.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. He appears to highlight in the middle of the section that there are some occurrences, and he lists them: "Criticisms of the army. Emergence of Chetnik ideology. Warnings to leave them alone" - that's presumably the army to leave them alone - "The assessment of some of their officers." And in this regard, the commander of the 2nd Military District will soon be talking to leaders of the Serbian people: Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Krajisnik, and Djukic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What do you make from the fact that there's no reference to the leaders of the HDZ talking to Kukanjac or the SDA talking to Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, he seems to be doing something in order to sort out what he sees as a potential problem in that he's going to meet these leaders, and he would seem to know who these leaders are. And he doesn't seem to be making much of a reference in the other two preceding paragraphs, A or B, necessarily that -- to dealing with them in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your -- let me direct your attention to paragraph 5. In paragraph 5 in the last sentence above subpart D, there's -- strike that. Paragraph 5 deals with volunteer units in the 2nd Military District zone. What is that referring to, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Part 5, as you say, deals with volunteers, and I think if you read the section in its entirety, which goes on to the following page, page 5, and highlights -- where it says "some experiences," it would appear to me reading that that the volunteers are those who are not JNA members, who have been mobilised into the JNA, but who put themselves or volunteered themselves in the district, in the -- in the districts and in the corps of the district. And I think if you read the second page, or page 5, it would appear that many if not most of these volunteers are Serbian volunteers. And importantly in -- maybe in part F, they -- well, they talk about the number of volunteers that are there. They then talk about the weapons that have been distributed to these volunteers. And the JNA have given some, and the SDS have given some. And I think the figure is 51.900 distributed by the JNA, 17.298 by the SDS. And then he -- he notes some experiences about these volunteers, in that many of them don't, I think, want to leave their municipalities. He talks about SDS leaders seeking weapons from the JNA and some other problems in that area. So I think the issue of volunteers are predominantly about Serbian volunteers who are working in the -- in the whole of the district.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Brown, what is your final conclusion in respect of this document? What does it reflect?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think it reflects, as I say in the report, by this date - and I think the date may be around about the 19th of March, even though it says "March" at the beginning - that there was this convergence and that the JNA in Bosnia and the 2nd Military District were working with the Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Serb leadership, and that they were providing weapons, and that there was this convergence by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if I can direct you to paragraph 1.12 in your report; that is found on page 15. In your report, you say - I quote - "By late April 1992, the JNA were in a position exclusively assisting the Bosnian Serbs and the SDS and any attempt at balance, if it had genuinely existed, had gone." Now, in April -- strike that. We see the reference earlier to the arming of volunteers, but by April were JNA forces, in fact, involved in combat operations supporting the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I am aware of some instances where that happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I was aware or am aware of the JNA assisting in Bosanska Krupa. I am aware that in Zvornik in early April 1992 there were -- there was JNA support from the 17th Corps, and I think I've made some references to that in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, we're going to be talking at length today and in the ensuing days about the 1st Krajina Corps, so I'd like to orient the Judges, if I could, to the geographic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, what about doing that after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour. Given the paucity of time and the number of exhibits I have to go through, I'm going to give you a very quick orientation of the are of the 1 KK, Your Honour. If we could turn to tab 5 of a -- of the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if you could do the same. Mr. Brown, briefly, what does this map depict?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I need you to turn your microphones on, Mr. Brown. There we are.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: This is a map that came from the 1st Krajina Corps archive. And although it's undated, it probably comes from late 1992, and -- or shows, depicts, the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps in its entirety. I know that it came probably from at least -- well, further on than October 1992 because the area of Jajce is under 1st Krajina Corps control, and that didn't happen until around about that time. Also the corridor was expanded slightly. So I'd assess that this map was from at least 1992. And it covers the zone of the corps and the sub-formations within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if Your Honours refer to your own map 527 on page 2 and Mr. Brown's report, footnotes 137 and 138.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you can confirm -- would you confirm for me that the municipalities that are wholly within the 1 KK area of responsibility on the 4th of June included Bosanska Dubica, Bosanska Gradiska, Srbac, Prijedor, Banja Luka, Laktasi, Prnjavor, Celinac, and Kotor Varos, and the municipalities that fell partially within the area of responsibility of the corps were Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most, Kljuc, Mrkonjic Grad, Sipovo, Jajce, Skender Vakuf, Travnik, Teslic, Doboj, Derventa, and Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's based on documentation that came from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could turn to the next exhibit, which is tab 6. And I'm sorry to rush through the orientation so quickly, Your Honours, but I've directed Your Honours to the appropriate municipalities and footnote in Mr. Brown's report. What I'd like to look at -- what I'd like to look at, Mr. Brown, is -- it is a separate binder, a small binder, and it is the analysis of combat readiness and activities of the Army of the Republika Srpska in 1992. This is a military secret, strictly confidential. It is dated on -- in April of 1993. Mr. Brown, is this an important military document, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I'd assess that it is an important military document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is and how it came to be created.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is another document that came from the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps. It's a document that's military secret, strictly confidential, which I believe is the highest classification of military documents in the VRS, and it's an analysis of combat -- or it's entitled "Analysis of the combat readiness and activities of the Army of the Republika Srpska in 1992." This document is -- appears to me both a reflection back on the activities of the army in 1992, an analysis of the current state of the army, as the document is dated in April 1993, and also highlights the areas that they need to improve in the -- in the coming period, as well as indicating some of the tasks that they are to -- to conduct in the -- in the coming period. So it's both a reflection on the state of the army, a reflection of what the army had achieved in 1992, and also a means by which they could address any weaknesses or problems and -- and also highlight the tasks that were to come. This type of document, I had seen one previously which was a JNA document in 1991, reflecting -- sorry, early 1992 reflecting back on 1991. So I can only assume that they kept up with this type of analysis, that it had been a JNA procedure to look back and to conduct some kind of analysis of how they were, and I believe the VRS continued with this in 1992. The document is very lengthy, and it's probably one of the most lengthy documents I think I saw in the archive of the 1st Krajina Corps that we had. And it's very detailed, and the index indicates all the various components of command and control and logistics and addresses each one individually. I'd also draw your attention to the section on page 4 and page 5, which is -- or appears to be a briefing plan with a schedule of speakers, and it in itself is quite detailed. And I believe this was probably a briefing either presenting this document or presenting the -- the main components of this document. And if you look at the -- the actual briefing of who attended it, it is all the very senior military figures of the VRS at the time and includes representatives from the government, representatives or men to brief from Yugoslavia, and Minister of Interior, I believe, also is pencilled in here on the briefing to conduct a speech. So I would assume that this plan was a briefing to present this document. The document itself, I believe, was compiled based on a request that had gone down from the VRS Main Staff earlier, in the early part of 1993. I'm aware that General Talic in the 1st Krajina Corps had received an order from the Main Staff to submit his own corps analysis, which he did do. I'm also aware of -- I think in the 2nd Krajina Corps, which is a neighbouring corps to General Talic, they had had the to do the same and I think that was around February 1003. So I assume that the Main Staff issued an instruction, the corps submitted the details, and then those details from the various corps were formed in this compiled report, which in essence was a report on the state of the army and how it -- how it had worked in 1992 and the state of play in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was this -- was this document, Mr. Brown, both objective on one hand and critical, on the other?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And -- and, in fact, it -- it does draw the -- the state of the army in its -- and the problems that it faced at the time, the problems it still had then, some of the weaknesses in the army that needed to be addressed, and although it is, obviously, on the other hand, it -- it discusses their successes too. And I think it's a key document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I want to direct your attention in this document to pages 28 to 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And while you're finding those pages -- Your Honours, this has been exhibited before as P64A and P529, Hanson tab 255.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I want to direct your attention to, specifically, and I'd like you to summarise, the role and importance of the communications system and its ability -- its capabilities as assessed by the army in 1992. Can you summarise those capabilities, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. This section deals with communications and signals, and I - - I think to some extent it's somewhat self-explanatory. They highlight that they had tasks to -- in order to -- to ensure continuous and safe functioning of command and reports could go up and down the chain. They had to establish a communications system, and that communications system had various components to it. It had a number of means by which information could be transmitted within the army and to other -- outside the army, as well, and they themselves assess this capability to be very good and that it was able to achieve its aim of -- they say one of the aims, anyway, was the prompt transmission of large quantities of information from the Main Staff of the army to the Supreme Command, subordinating elements, participating units and contacts with a view to the swiftest possible notification and informing -- and feedback in the form of directive decisions and orders. And the summary that they have at the end, they do discuss that there were some difficulties, but the summary that they have was that communications was very -- were very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in this particular segment of the report - for example, on page 33, a radio relay communications - it indicates in the second paragraph on page 33 under that heading that they had radio relay communications with simultaneous translation of information through 523 communication channels consisting of 416 telephone and 107 telegraph channels. They also describe, do they not, in this report that they had radio communications, wire service, courier service, and they describe the encryption capabilities of the communications in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, they do. They highlight each of those sections, and they also talk about -- within -- within that broad range of communications that they had to assist other users outside the army, as well. But yes, those were the main means that they discuss in this -- in this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, Mr. Brown, to figure 4 on page 36.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- in this section, they're talking about wire services ask. That means both hardwire communications between two communicators, but also they use the PTT system, which was the civilian telephone line. And this particular chart outlines, as it says, the use of PTT and military automatic telephone exchanges outside the army of the RS. And it just lists -- so basically it was a system -- it wasn't a military communications system per se, but they utilised that to communicate. I'm not a communications expert particularly, but I'd imagine each of the numbers here is either links to an individual line or a telephone exchange or a telephone handset and a number of lines going into the various formations, including the Supreme Command, Main Staff, the corps, all the other units of the army, some logistic components, military hospital, TV SRNA, press centres, and the warning and reporting centre. And it -- it lists here the PTT lines and also the PTT from Belgrade. So they used Belgrade PTT links, as well, in some cases to try and ensure communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, can I direct your attention to the table that appears on the next page, which is actually figure 5.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. This particular section deals with encrypted and encoded communications or telegraph communications, and the particular section talks about the amount of written communications or encrypted telegrams that were passed predominantly in the army. It also makes mention of the Pale warning and reporting centre of the government. The warning and reporting system, I believe, was a system that the JNA had established, which was to do with national defence. I think the VRS simply utilised that existing system. And there was obviously a Pale and warning and reporting centre, which from this would indicate that the government was utilising that system. And a number of encrypted or encoded telegrams, I think two or three are highlighted here, seemed to have been established or used during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the -- your review of this particular portion of the report on the army permit you to come to a conclusion as to whether or not the army had the technical means by which to communicate with the civilian leadership over the -- who were above the army itself?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I -- I would say from this, yes, that they had the means to -- to do that. There is some indication that they had connections outside the army, that they had to establish some connections outside the army, and they themselves, I think, assessed that the -- that the communications system in 1992 was very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, did you -- if you'd turn to tab -- tabs 7 and 8 of the folder. If you'd look at tab 7. This is a previous exhibit. It's an intercepted communication. It's a previous Prosecution exhibit, P292, P389A, P389A.1 and 389B. This is a communication between Mr. Krajisnik and an individual by the name of Radivoje Grkovic, and Mr. Grkovic is identified on page 2 of the intercepted communication as being the Nedzarici Battalion commander. And if you will turn to tab 8, which is -- this is also an intercepted communication between Mr. Krajisnik and an individual by the name of Milan Kovic. This has been previously exhibited as 292 KID 39219, and this is dated the 21st of April 1992. And it's a conversation where Mr. Krajisnik is inquiring in getting a report as to the military situation in Grbavica and in other parts of Sarajevo. Now, does this confirm for you that the -- that the technical capabilities --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to leading of this nature. In fact, the -- the entire prelude to the question and the nature of the question are at a level of objectionable leading, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then I won't lead, Your Honour. I'll ask a different -- I'll form the question differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What does this suggest to you, Mr. Brown, in respect of the communication capabilities permitting the senior political leadership to inquire with battalion commanders and in respect of the military situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, based on these two -- two transcripts, it would appear that Mr. Krajisnik had an ability to speak to low-level commanders in order to avail himself of the situation in the territory. It would seem -- if the - - if the intercept is -- is as it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let me return to the report on the army, and let me direct your attention, if I can, to page 153.
