I'm going to read -- I'm going to read to you the portion of this report on the army, page 153, paragraph 4, and then I'm going to read another section to you. This paragraph at 153 is a paragraph taken from the concluding remarks of Dr. Radovan Karadzic on the 5th of April, 1993, in which he says in paragraph 4, "The Supreme Command as a whole, as well as every individual member of the Supreme Command, was informed of the objectives of planned operations and concerted battles and of their results frequently in great detail. This demonstrates that control and command of the Army of Republika Srpska is united and that it is based upon a high degree of concurrence and unity in selecting the targets of each individual operation or battle and in assigning tasks to individual operational and tactical formations." Can you comment on Dr. Karadzic's remarks that I've just read.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think the remarks probably speak for themselves, and -- and Karadzic obviously believes that the Supreme Command was not only informed but took part in the planning of operations and -- in some detail and had an ability to do that. I would assume that if the communication system hadn't been functioning, that the -- that would have hampered that process, and he himself seems to be admitting here that -- that that was -- these objectives were planned operations, reports, and that was linked to command and control. And from the law on the army, I know that was also a function of the commander-in-chief, so it would seem to be self-evident that he was briefed on operations and took an active part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let me direct you to pages 8 and 9 of this same report, again dealing with the issue of communications. I want to read you the paragraph -- the last paragraph on page 8, continuing over to page 9. "The command. Report and command liaison links. Warning and notification functions were well organised in communications plans, with appropriate documents and data, were precise so that it was possible on the basis of these to establish the planned communication links. With a high degree of certainty, we can say that the existing communication system meets the needs of command, coordination, and reporting needs at all levels from the Supreme Command, the Supreme Commander, the General Staff, to the lower levels." I invite your comments, Mr. Brown, as to that paragraph I have just read.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to echo what Mr. Karadzic had said, and -- and this particular component was presumably the army's perspective and not Dr. Karadzic's perspective, and -- and it seems to echo very much what they said, and also replicate the issue of communications, that communications were very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, I'd like to come back to page 153 of this report, paragraph 4, and I'd like to focus your attention on the second paragraph contained in paragraph 4. "The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska has performed the functions of the staff of the Supreme Command and at the same time that of the superior command for operational and some joint tactical formations, which presupposed the agreement of the Supreme Command in respect of all tasks and objectives of the armed struggle. This relationship between the command structures and the organs of government and the Supreme Command made it impossible for the Main Staff to make decisions absolutely on its own. Rather, every operational battle was politically endorsed on the basis of the interests of the Serbian people and approved by the highest authorities of Republika Srpska." Mr. Brown, can I again invite your comments and observations on that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think this would indicate very much this issue of unity of command and that there wasn't a division between what the military were trying to do or doing and their wider political objectives of the Bosnian Serbs. I think it highlights that by that comment, and I think there are other documents that would -- would seem to echo that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "unity of command," Mr. Brown, can you be more precise, more explicit? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, very much that there was not a divergence here, that there was -- there was a very close relationship, that the political leadership in essence were -- were giving overall guidance to the military, and that all decisions and operational battles were -- were politically endorsed by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention, Mr. Brown, on essentially how orders were transmitted from the highest levels down and from the lowest levels of the army back up to the highest levels with -- up to the political leadership. And if I could first of all, Mr. Brown, ask you -- if we could turn to page 159 of the army report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question because things -- we are moving very quickly. Could we come back to page 9, please, and to the third and fourth line. [In English] "And reporting needs at all levels from the Supreme Command, the Supreme Commander, the General Staff, to lower levels." [Interpretation] I would like to understand what "Supreme Command" means and what "Supreme Commander" also means. What do these words actually mean, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was aware that in late 1992 the Supreme Command was established, I believe, in November; although, I'd have to say I defer to those who have done political analysis more. But I would believe that what they're talking about here is the Supreme Command, the Supreme Commander probably being Dr. Karadzic, the General Staff being the Main Staff, and the lower levels being the corps and probably subordinated formations of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But is there a difference between the Supreme Command, on the one side, and the Supreme Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to defer to someone who might know more about the -- the law on the regulations and the political leadership. But it may well mean here the Supreme Command is a corporate body and the Supreme Commander being the president of the republic or Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, again, using this same document, if we could turn to page 159. And, first of all, very generically, can you identify the various ways in which orders were conveyed in the VRS from the top, from the political leadership down through the Main Staff and down through -- to the lower echelons? Just identify the various ways in which that was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, just in relation to that, I think the witness has quite clearly indicated even as recently as the last question that he would defer to those who have done political analysis more. That's page 53, line 10. And it's quite clear from the beginning of his evidence in chief in relation to the limitations of his evidence -- it's clear that this is an analysis on military developments in the Krajina for a certain year period. This witness is simply not in a position to answer the question that Mr. Harmon has asked him in relation to the -- particularly in relation to -- from political leadership down through the Main Staff, in my submission, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I disagree with that, Your Honour, because this report indicates precisely the manners in which these orders are directed down. The question is, Can you tell us the very -- identify the various ways in which orders were conveyed? And I can direct Your Honours' attention to paragraph 1 -- I'm sorry, page 159, specifically referencing oral orders from the president of the republic as the Supreme Commander of the forces did orally assign a number of tasks. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness what he knows. Do you have any -- Ms. Loukas has drawn the attention to the fact that your report is in certain respects limited. Now, we are talking here -- the question is dealing with, I take it, orders of a military nature and suggests that it came from the political leadership, where it, well, at least comes at a borderline of -- because we have heard some evidence that Mr. Karadzic was the Supreme Commander, which makes him both a political figure and a military figure. Are you able to answer that question since it comes at the edge of what seems to be your expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- again, I would defer very much to people who were in the political analysis sphere, but I am aware of documentation that I have reviewed, including some political documents of a military nature, that indicate that there were directives, that there were meetings. This document indicates oral orders being assigned. I am aware of meetings that occurred, and I am aware of some documentation of reports that go up the chain, as well. And so I am in part aware of -- of -- of meetings that occurred, minutes of meetings, schedule briefings. The 16th Assembly Session, for example, is another example -- you know, Mladic was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to expand on that at this moment. I do understand your answer to be that although it is about political leaders, that it does not necessarily go beyond the field you studied and beyond your expertise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I am aware of military documents that make reference to this issue of the chain of command and the passage of information down and up the chain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you may answer the question put to you. Perhaps, Mr. Harmon, it would be wise to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you summarise, and then we'll explore each particular detail -- Mr. Brown, can you summarise the -- the means in which orders were conveyed from the Supreme Commander and political leaders to the Main Staff, members of the Main Staff, and down through the lower echelons of the 1st Krajina Corps and the army.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, this document indicates oral orders as being a means of communication. I'm aware of Presidency sessions in which members of the military were present, according to the minutes of the meetings. I'm aware of references in this document that strategic objectives led to the issuance of directives from the military, and I'm aware of a functioning chain of command within the military down to the lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, Mr. Brown, to an intercepted radio - - a telephone communication that is found in tab 10. This is P -- Prosecution Exhibit 67, tab 32, and also P292, KID 31423. This is an intercepted radio communication, Mr. Brown, between General Mladic and Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik dated the 27th of May, 1992. And if you turn to page 2 of this intercept, you see a conversation wherein Mr. -- General Mladic says, "I'm going further as planned, and tomorrow I will stop by to get new instructions." Mr. Krajisnik responds, "Excellent." General Mladic says, "So we'll arrange for what we should do next." And Mr. Krajisnik says, "All right." Can I have your observations as to this particular intercept, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, again, if the intercept transcript is -- is accurate, it would seem to be that a senior member of the Bosnian Serb leadership was able to speak to Ratko Mladic and -- and give him instructions, and that would seem to -- seem to show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I seem to be missing the English translation of tab 9. Mr. Brown, does the English translation of tab 9 appear to be in your binder?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Is this the one on the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Without having it in front of me -- it is. Actually I have the B/C/S version in front of me, but I don't have the English version, so let me just get the English version. Now, is this -- is this, Mr. Brown, an illustration of a -- an order in writing from the 1st Krajina command to other members within the army?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a -- an order that General Talic sent out on the 21st of May to his subordinate units in the corps, and it's -- it's an order on general mobilisation. And the order starts by saying, "A decision of the Serbian Republic of BH Presidency on the 20th of May has initiated general mobilisation of all citizens of the Serbian Republic." And then he goes on in his order to identify what that means in his corps. And I'll draw your attention to point 1, which is, "To immediately establish direct contact with municipal and military and territorial organs on the ground, offering expert and material support for the mobilisation process." The end discusses issues about mobilising conscripts. If I draw your attention to point 6: "Explain to conscripts on their -- as they arrive the goals of our struggle, and brief them on their rights and duties." And then in paragraph 8, he states that "Until units receive concrete combat tasks," presumably meaning that they're expecting some combat action in the forthcoming weeks, "engage them in the following tasks." And point 4: "Establish the closest possible cooperation with the people and legal authorities within their zones of responsibility." The -- point 11, the orders that they're "not to allow the presence of any paramilitary formations or other special organisations within the zone." And that these people are to be dispersed -- or "disperse individual members," presumably meaning paramilitary formations or special organisations, "amongst the units as volunteers. If they refuse, break them up, and if necessary, destroy them." And then he orders that unit commanders of units are directly responsible for implementing these assignments, and this order is disseminated to all the various components of his corps, that distribution list of the units within his corps. And this document to me would seem to indicate that there was a decision at the highest level of the Presidency on the 20th of May. That was then disseminated down the chain. General Talic was disseminating that down to chain to his subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 8 of the report on the army once again, Mr. Brown, and in the second paragraph in the middle of that paragraph, it says, "The main documents used to regulate the utilisation of forces at Main Staff level were directives." And earlier in your testimony, you mentioned directives, and you also mentioned directives in your expert report on page 169 of paragraph 3.27. What is a directive, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: A directive is a large planning construction or -- or order that deals generally with the higher level military -- military planning, and these were used by the VRS throughout the war, not just in 1992. I'm aware of four directives pushed out by the VRS in 1992, and there were a number of other directives that were subsequently pushed out in the following years, but they are, in essence, large military high-level planning orders to subordinate corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if we can turn to page 159 of the military report, the analysis, once again. Let me read to you from the second paragraph. It says, "The strategic objectives of our war which were promptly defined and set before the Main Staff of the Army of the RS, the commands and units, served as a general guideline upon which we planned the actual operations and concerted battles. This means that objectives were set before us rather than specific tasks spelled out; although, the president of the republic is the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the RS did orally assign a number of tasks which were general and vital significance to our struggle and protecting the Serbian people and its territories. The Main Staff of the Army of RS translated the set of objectives and tasks into general and individual missions of the Army of the RS and the individual, operational, and tactical formations with the goals of every individual, combat action, operation, or battle being specifically defined." Can you comment on this particular passage in the army report, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think that is a -- a fairly accurate reflection of -- of how at the higher level these -- these goals were disseminated into the VRS Main Staff, and then from the earlier quote, that they took those objectives, wrote them into directives, and those directives were passed down the chain to subordinate corps, and the objectives, I would argue, in this reference and elsewhere relate to the objectives that were stated in the 16th Assembly Session on the 12th of May. And I'm aware in the two directives that we have from 1992 that there are a number of references that directly link -- it would appear to directly link the objectives, the strategic objectives articulated at that Assembly session that are in the military objectives of the VRS. And furthermore, I would argue that the operational activity certainly in the area that I know reasonably well, the 1st Krajina Corps, the operational activity that they conducted can be directly linked to those strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Brown, if we could turn to tab 11, which has been previously exhibited as P727, and also in the Brcko dossier as tab 15. Is this one of the directives that you have referred to? Is this ...?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, this is operational directive 3, which was written in, I believe, the 3rd of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And generally speaking, these directives, they came from the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think this one is signed by -- or it's got Mladic's signature block, I believe. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did this objective -- did this directive, Mr. Brown, as set forth on pages 4 and 5, go to the subordinate corps, including the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it -- I'll just check the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring specifically to paragraphs 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, and 5.5.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. It would appear that all the various corps of the Main Staff were given tasks. I'm not sure if this one actually has a distribution list. And it may well be because this was on the dissemination -- the dissemination means, maybe the use of telegraph or whatever, but I am aware of General Talic reacting to this directive because, I believe, not long afterwards, in fact, a day or so afterwards, he himself wrote his own corps-level instruction. But this is an example of a directive, and it does go to give various tasks to the corps within the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You referenced earlier, Mr. Brown, that these directives were -- were centred around -- or involved the strategic objectives that had been announced at the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Can you direct the Court's attention to references within this document dealing specifically with the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: The strategic objectives -- well, for example, the strategic objective 5, which related to Sarajevo, Karadzic announced that they were to divide Sarajevo, they were to control their territory of Sarajevo, and they were all to -- also to ensure that forces in Sarajevo were not going to be moved to other areas that were of some importance. He also mentioned at the 16th Assembly Session that they had encircled Sarajevo. And when you go to the task that's given to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in this directive - and there are references there - that they are to maintain this blockade of -- of Sarajevo and prevent its breaking. And I would argue that in order to stop forces, Muslim and Croat forces in Sarajevo from going to other areas that were of importance to the Bosnian Serbs, that the way to do that would be to blockade the city and make sure they didn't come out. And that would seem to be one link in this directive that the task being given to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps related to an objective that was articulated by Karadzic at the 12th of May. There are other references. I think -- I have to go through --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, Mr. Brown, to page 3, third paragraph from the bottom, where it deals with an advance on the left bank of the River Neretva.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. That was another objective that Karadzic had stated. I think it was Operation Strategic Goal Number 4, establish a border on the Una and Neretva Rivers. And I think if you look at what the Herzegovina Corps was tasked to do here, which was the corps that covered the Neretva area -- Herzegovina Corps used part of the forces to prevent penetration from the territory of Croatia, Western Herzegovina, and direct operations of the main forces towards the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, can I direct your attention to paragraph 5.1, where there is a reference to the Posavina and the main forces carrying out offensive operations in the Posavina. Do you see that reference, under "Tasks of units"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. The 1st Krajina Corps had actually already established a corridor in the Posavina area, which was strategic goal number 2. They had achieved that goal by early July 2002. But in this, this is August, so it's a little bit later, but what they had to do was expand that corridor so they could get to the river. And the Krajina Corps here was given -- given that task, in essence, of protecting the corridor. So I would argue this is a directive which would relate back to these strategic goals as articulated on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what do the documentation show, Mr. Brown, in respect of a directive being sent from the Main Staff to the corps level? What happened, then, at the corps level?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I know that this directive, in particular directive 3, General Talic issued his own corps-wide instruction. I'm aware of another example. We don't have directive 1 or 2, or at least we don't when I was working here with the OTP, but there are examples when a directive came out in June and General Talic issued his own corps-wide instruction based on that directive. And I'm aware that an operational directive 4 which followed that the corps followed those directives and issued their own corps-wide instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask you to speak slower and think of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, we're going to have to pause, or I'm going to have to slow down. I don't know if I can go any slower in my manner of speech. But if we could turn, Mr. Brown, to tab 12. Can you identify the document in tab 12.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Tab 12 was another directive. It's operational directive number 4., dated 19th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document that comes from the Main Staff of the army to the subordinate corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I -- while we were discussing the strategic objectives, Mr. Brown, can you turn to page 2 of this particular document. In the middle, the paragraph that starts with "Most of the tasks carried out in full, and amongst the most significant we would stress the following." Can you tell the Judges what this passage means.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: This passage would seem to be a reflection on what they had already achieved, and I think it echoes my point that the strategic objectives that had been announced at the 12th of May formed -- or the military worked to those objectives. And here they are highlighting where they managed to achieve some successes in relation to those. So, for example, the 1st Krajina Corps had preserved the corridor through the Posavina. That was strategic goal number 2. 2nd Krajina corp is successfully defending the north-west border of the republic on the Una River; the Una River was an objective that Karadzic announced at the 12th of May. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had fully established command and control and prevented the lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo. Again, I would argue that that links to what Karadzic had said in relation to the strategic goal number 5 about Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indeed the -- number 3, the East Bosnia Corps is to preserve the corridor, which was also another strategic objective; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, the East Bosnia Corps was also involved in securing the corridor. It wasn't just the 1st Krajina Corps, but it was the neighbouring corps of the East Bosnia Corps. So they moved from opposite directions to secure the corridor, and that was achieved in July, the very few days -- first few days of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if we turn to the next page, there's a reference at the top to the following tasks from directive 3, which we have just seen, not being carried out. Can you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think here they're -- although they initially said we've achieved some success, they -- they haven't completely carried out the tasks from number 3, directive number 3. In particular, the towns of Gorazde, Gradacac, Maglaj, Bugojno, Olovo, and Orasje have not been liberated. The Posavina Corridor, although it had been achieved, had not been successfully widened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I say it in English, is it then better, instead of in French, to make it clear to the interpreters that it is very sorry for them, my words being described to Judge Hanoteau in the transcript. But could I please ask you to really slow down. It's -- the interpreters cannot follow it in that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise to you, Your Honour, and also to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mainly to the interpreters, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And number 4, the Herzegovina Corps had failed to reach the Neretva River, which, again, Karadzic had said was a strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'm listening to the French interpretation, so I'm going to pause until that is completed. But if -- could you turn, Mr. Brown, to page 4 of this document. Again, approximately seven lines down there's a reference to the left bank of the Neretva River, and there's also a reference to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you please. I'm sorry. But I have a question to ask. It's going extremely fast, Mr. Harmon, right? It's going very, very fast. So I'd like to be really sure that I've understood everything. When the witness is talking about Mr. Karadzic's decision, is it a decision made by Mr. Karadzic himself or by the civilian authorities or the Assembly? I'd like to really understand what is meant by "decision made by Mr. Karadzic." Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe the word "decision" was not -- not the most appropriate, then. What I'm just referring to are the announcements at the 16th Assembly Session on the 12th of May that he made in relation to what the wider strategic goals of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Witness. I'm reading what's on the transcript. When I see "decision made by Mr. Karadzic," is it a decision made by Karadzic himself, or is it a decision that he had the Assembly enforce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I believe that at this 16th Assembly Session Radovan Karadzic announced the strategic goals, and he articulated that those strategic goals had been formulated by the government, the Presidency, the Council for National Security, and he articulated those at that session, and that is what I'm -- I mean by that. Now, who composed those bodies and what they're composed of, I think I would rather defer to somebody who's involved in political analysis. But what I mean is that Radovan Karadzic announced those goals and articulated who had been involved in the formulation of those goals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'd like just to direct your attention again to the portion at the top of page 4, where there is a reference to "reaching the left bank of the Neretva," and then later in that same paragraph, "gaining access to the sea." That again is another reference to the strategic objectives; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the rest of this document. On that page 4, it says, "The tasks of the units," and thereafter, between subparts A through subparts F, found at page 6, those units he's giving the tasks to are identified; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That includes the 1st Krajina Corps and the other corps under the command of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we turn to page 5 of this directive, under D, "the Drina Corps," it says, "From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad (the dam), Zvornik and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Bilac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population. First off are the able-bodied men and armed men to surrender, and if they refuse, destroy them." That reference to "force the Muslim population to leave," does that relate to a strategic objective, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the question in the nature of the way that Mr. Harmon has formulated. Firstly, in relation to its -- its leading form. And -- and secondly, Your Honour -- yes, in essence it's the leading, Your Honour. I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I think Mr. Harmon has four or five times asked whether portions of this document relate to certain strategic goals. What's different now, and in what way exactly is it leading?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Harmon reads out a portion of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- and says, "That reference, does that relate to a strategic objective?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer can only be a yes or no. That's a classic leading question, in that respect. That's the first aspect. The other -- the mere fact, Your Honour, that I haven't objected to a question formed in the previous in that manner does not mean that I'm disentitled to objecting from this particular question, Your Honour, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: We're talking about something that refers to the Neretva River, the Una River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas -- yes, Ms. Loukas, I have always understood that a leading question is a question which either suggests the answer to be given or a question that suggests something that has not yet been established. That's, at least, in accordance with ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It does suggest the answer. The answer is, "Yes, that does relate to a strategic objective."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or no, it does not relate to any strategic objective, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, we'll see what his answer is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, to say it doesn't relate to anything at all, this, of course, would not be a question, which would make much sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I guarantee you the answer is yes, Your Honour. Let's see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this is unfair, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is unfair. You might know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know the answer. Okay. Well, then, Mr. Harmon, you may proceed. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: The answer is I do believe it does -- it does link -- it links -- I would argue to strategic objective number 3, which was to establish a corridor in the Drina, the Drina River or the Drina Valley, and those areas, Bila, Zepa, Gorazde fall within that area. And I would also argue that along with other documentation and other material and -- which I've included in my report, that the reference to forcing them to leave together with the Muslim population is tied to strategic goal number 1, about separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, let me direct your attention -- Mr. Brown, let me direct your attention to tabs -- bear with me for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Can I just possibly comment on one other aspect of this directive if that's okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- I do not mind. Mr. Harmon has to use his time in the best ways of ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very briefly, if I can draw your attention to page 6, and in relation to the use of the Air Force. It states here that, "The use of aircraft can be ordered by, one, members of the Presidency of the Republika Srpska/the Supreme Command; two, commander of the army of the Republika Srpska; and three, Chief of the Main Staff of the army." That -- I just wanted to flag that up as maybe of some importance when we were discussing that earlier issue of whether leadership or the political leadership or the Presidency have any relationship with the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, finally in respect of this document, because I'm going to refer to the number in the next two exhibits, directive 4 at the top left- hand corner bears the number 02/5, and can -- I turn -- direct your attention to tabs 13 and 13.1. Mr. Brown, can you tell the Court what the exhibits found under tabs 13 and 13.1 are. Let me just -- I'm sorry. I have the wrong number. 13.1 -- I'm sorry, I have the wrong number. 13.1, Mr. Brown, and 14. What are those documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: 13.1 is a Drina Corps command document entitled "Decision for further activities," and it comes shortly after directive 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, Mr. Brown, to paragraph 1 in both of those exhibits, 13.1 and 14, please. Do you see a reflection in the first paragraph of those respective documents to directive 4?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And the reference to forcing the Muslim population to leave the area is similar to that found in the quoted document, which is directive 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in summary, are documents 13.1 and the document in 14, both of these documents are issued by Commander Colonel Milenko Zivanovic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: At the time he was the Drina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And are both these documents that I've just referred to orders that flow from the commander of the Drina Corps to subordinate units within the Drina Corps? If I look and I direct your attention in paragraph -- in document 13.1, this is directed to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade command, and in document 14 directed to the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. These are two subordinate units of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this -- these are military orders.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, and I think if you take the documents together, they show a functioning chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I -- in both of -- both of these tabs, 13.1 and the document in 14, can we turn to -- we'll just take 13.1 to page 4, under the portion of "Morale and psychological preparations." That's found at subpart C. It says, "Prior to starting any activities, members of the unit are to be informed about the significant aim of the activity. It is to be pointed out that the achieving of the goals of the Serb people, that is, the creation of the Serb state in these areas, depends on the outcome of small actions and on the outcome of the entire operation." Can you comment on that, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's of some -- some note that they reference the goals and that this is being passed down to the lowest formation of the army; these are not issues that are kept at a high level. And the -- the fact that they're talking about small actions as having an important -- an importance is -- is of some note. It, again, re-emphasises to me that the strategic goals and the goals articulated were important; they were related and ended up with military action on the ground, and they were disseminated down through the military chain to the lowest level. This is a brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'd like you to quickly look at the documents that are found in tabs 15 through 19, that all reference a number, 2-126, dated the 24th of November, 1992. If you'd look at each of those documents and tell the Judges what these documents are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, for me, also, sometimes it goes a bit too quick. I would like to take the witness back to 13.1 and 14, if you would not mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "Can I direct your attention, Mr. Brown, to paragraph 1 in both of those exhibits. Do you see a reflection in the first paragraph of those respective documents relating to directive 4?" And the answer of the witness was, "Yes, I do. And the reference of forcing the Muslim population to leave the area is similar to that found in the quoted document, which is directive 4." Paragraph 1 is rather lengthy, so I would like to invite the witness to tell me exactly where in paragraph 1 - and let's start with 13.1 - where it says that -- "forcing the Muslim population to leave the area." Could you please -- because it's two pages, so I have not found it yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, when I say it's similar -- paragraph 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- states, "Wear the enemy out, break it up or force it to surrender, and force the Muslim population" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- to leave the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I found it. Most of the lines were about enemies, but here it's clearly the population. Yes. And in 14, yes, it's the same: "Force the Muslim population" -- I found it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I was asking you to identify what the documents are that are contained in tabs 15 through 19.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: These would appear, at face value, to be receipts for that Drina Corps instruction, the Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade command and a number of other receipts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this is a reflection of the orders going from the top, from the directive, to the corps command, down to the brigade command, and down to the lower units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, if we could turn to tab 20, a document that is dated January 23rd, 1993, signed by the commander of the corps -- the Drina Corps, Colonel Milenko Zivanovic. And this is an operation -- a combat order, so -- and it's an order directed to the commands of all corps units. And if I could direct your attention, Mr. Brown, to the top of page 8. It is a continuation from the -- the morale and psychological preparation, and it says, "Transport to other areas must be provided for the civilian population of the enemy, and those who accept the authority of the Republika Srpska are to be disarmed and returned to their homes." So when there's a reference in this to transport to other areas the civilian population, can you comment on that, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I would imagine here what they're talking about is moving them to areas outside of the places that they were -- they were living.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Your Honour, as a contextual document, since directive 4 dealt with the Drina Corps in the area of Zepa and Cerska, I have included for Your Honours the report from Mr. Mazowiecki dated the 5th of May, 1993. Yes, tab -- it's found in tab 21, and it outlines in part -- or describes in part the operation General -- General Zivanovic and the Drina Corps were involved in. Not all parts are relevant, but there are selected paragraphs in here that are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Brown, we will move on, and I'm interested in having you generally describe, based on the documentation that you've seen, and how it was that the army reported to the highest civilian structures in the Republika Srpska. How did they do that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: From the Krajina Corps documents that I've reviewed, there was a very detailed reporting chain that ran from brigade level, low-level units of the corps, to the corps command. General Talic issued instructions that brigades were to report twice a day. I know that there were notebooks and documents at the corps command in which references were made to brigade activity. The 1st Krajina Corps itself was ordered to send combat reports, regular combat reports, and in the documents that I reviewed in 1992, the 1st Krajina Corps generally sent two reports a day, sometimes three, and infrequently one. I don't remember of one day in 1992 that the 5th Corps, when it was the 5th Corps/1st Krajina Corps did not send a daily combat report to its superior formation. Those regular combat reports were all structured in the same way, covering enemy activity, situation on the territory, logistic issues, manning issues, and any special problems that had arisen. Those daily combat reports, when the 1st Krajina Corps was established, went to the VRS Main Staff. And as I say, they generally went two and sometimes -- or very frequently twice -- three times. There were occasionally special reports that they sent up to the Main Staff; I saw a small -- a small number of those. I saw some documentary evidence that related to briefings that the corps commanders had to give. I know of one example in documentary evidence that was a briefing to the senior political leadership that the corps commanders had to give in, I believe, early June 1992. There were requests for maps occasionally. And those were some of the ways that I know that the reports went from the ground through the corps up to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, do we take a break at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do take a break at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- approximately this time. We'll have a break for 20 minutes and resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Harmon, there would be a possibility to sit tomorrow and the day after tomorrow in the morning. I also am aware that that sometimes creates problems as far as visiting Mr. Krajisnik is concerned. Therefore, I inquire with the parties whether that would be something they would support or object.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can indicate it's something I would not support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think that's a sufficient reason to remain in the afternoon. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, what I'd be interested in hearing from you is what your -- what the documents that you reviewed showed as to how the army, either at the corps level or at the Main Staff level, communicated to the civilian structures, the Presidency and the political leaders above them.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I am aware of some documentary evidence that would highlight some of the methods in which they were able to communicate to the senior -- senior political leadership. If we -- or if I draw your attention to the report on the army in 1993, there are a number of references in that document that would indicate that there was a good communication between the -- the army and the senior political leadership. Page -- page 9, which we have already seen before, "With a high degree of certainty we can say that the existing communications system meets the needs of command, coordination, and reporting needs at all levels from Supreme Command, Supreme Commander, and General Staff." We've seen that before. Page 13, the fourth bullet down, under the general heading of "Control and command functions," "which have been implemented through the establishment and maintenance of permanent and mutually beneficial cooperation with the authorities, the SDS, the Serbian Orthodox Church at all levels." Page 29, we've seen before, which was the issue of communications and the signals units, and they were set the task of the prompt transmission of large quantities of information from the Main Staff of the army to the Supreme Command, subordinated elements, and so on. And they later on say that they -- they had judged that they had been able to meet those tasks and that the corps' signal system and communication was very good. Page 153, we've seen that -- that one before, as well, I think, from Dr. Karadzic, who himself articulated that "The Supreme Command as a whole, as well as every individual member of the Supreme Command, were informed of the objectives of planned operations, concerted battles, and their results frequently in great detail." So this document would seem to highlight that there -- there was a -- a relationship between the military -- that both the military are saying that it functioned, Dr. Karadzic said that it functioned. But I am aware of other documentation, some documentation that would indicate meetings, the Presidency session, minutes which discussed military or defence-related issues, the briefing of members of that -- those -- those sessions by military officers. And so there are -- there is other documentation in it that would seem to echo what was said in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have selected a number of Presidency session minutes that Mr. Brown has reviewed. Those are found in tabs 22 through 36 of the binders. They -- it splits between binder 1 and binder 2. I shall not go through all of those items, but I'd like to direct Mr. Brown's attention to three of those session minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you present the other as contextual exhibits, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They're already in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're already in evidence. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've forgotten to check on the list. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could, Mr. Brown, in the first binder, if we could start with tab 24 of the first binder in front of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just want to indicate to the Court in relation to the documents that Mr. Harmon's referring to -- and when one looks at the exhibit list associated with these binders, I can indicate that I first became aware of these political exhibits when I got this list when I came into court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. I'm not sure when that list was sent to Ms. Loukas. These exhibits I'm referring to are old exhibits. They have been the subject of examination and cross-examination in Mr. Treanor's evidence. These are documents that I believe Ms. Loukas has in front of her at the very moment we're talking. These documents are not a mystery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's not the only criterion, whether it's a mystery or not. Is it material used in the footnotes in the report? Could we perhaps ask the witness the minutes of the Presidency sessions. Are they footnoted material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they're not in the report, Your Honour. I'd have to check again. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- at the very end they could have been, but I'm not sure if they are. I don't think they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: However, Your Honour there, is reference to direct communication and information to the higher-ups in and throughout the report of the army, in Mr. Brown's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, it's to be preferred, Mr. Harmon, that if you want to -- I mean, the material is of such a volume by now that -- if it were only for Ms. Loukas to find the material and bring it with her -- and I'm not saying this because that's, of course, not the main issue because we could present it on the ELMO. But for preparation purpose, it's good if these lists -- I mean, just looking at this list, whether it bears a date or not ... Well, let's see what happens, but it's clear that this is not the best way to do it. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps I'm -- may I ask you another question: Do I understand from your present position that you would live not too far away from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're very correct, Your Honour; I don't live too far away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That at least, Ms. Loukas, if it would finally cause you major problems, would make a decision when needed to recall the witness on this material easier than it would be if he would live in --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. But I can -- I just very briefly want to indicate for the record that, of course, my preparation was based on the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's based on -- and, of course, I went through all the documents and footnotes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but Ms. Loukas, I think I've been clear enough until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if we could turn to the 24th -- tab 24. And I'm going to refer to two other tabs, and then I'm going to ask you some questions. This 5th Session of the Presidency was held on the 10th of June, indicates that members of -- that the following members were present: Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Plavsic, Dr. Koljevic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Branko Djeric. And it says, "At the beginning of the session, the Presidency reviewed information received during the night on the situation at the front and reports of the international public foreign press?" And if we turn to tab 32 - that's found in the second binder - the beginning of the second binder. Mr. Brown, this is the -- this is -- these are the minutes of the 21st Session of the Presidency. They were held on the 2nd of August, 1992, and it says at the top that the session was attended by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Dr. Miljana, as printed, Plavsic, Dr. Nikola Koljevic, Lieutenant Ratko Mladic, and it also refers to Mr. Krajisnik as being present, although not in the top paragraph. In item 1 - -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if you would look at the original, perhaps that might ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not have the original, unfortunately, in front of me in this binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, from what I see, it's tab 32 on the original. If I look at the names at the top, it's Radovan Karadzic, Miljana - so that means that it's the same document with the same mistake - Dr. Nikola Koljevic, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, and then comes Ratko Mladic and Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I invite the parties to correct this obvious mistake. Ms. Loukas, I take it that you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, absolutely, Your Honour. I've checked the B/C/S version myself, and it's quite apparent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we turn to item 2 on the second page, Mr. Brown, it says, "On the basis of the condition and assessment of the political situation presented, Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic briefed those present on the assessment of the military situation in Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, describing the situation in each combat sector, the necessary tasks, and the connection between ensuring material potentials and financial resources and the necessity of adopting the decision on general mobilisation." At the end of that paragraph, it also discusses that the president of the republic should issue an order, a proclamation on general mobilisation. And the final one of these minutes I'd like to refer you to is found in tab 35.1. This has previously been exhibited as P64. This is the 22nd Session of the Presidency held on the 31st of August, 1992. The Presidency session -- the session was attended by the following members of the Presidency: Dr. Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Dr. Biljana Plavsic, Dr. Branko Djeric, and Dr. Nikola Koljevic and Dr. -- I'm sorry, Deputy Prime Minister Milan Trbojevic." If we go to the bottom of page 1 of the English translation, it says, "During the session of the Presidency, representatives of the army of the Serbian Republic, Colonel General Ratko Mladic and Major General Milan Gvero arrived. Generals briefed the Presidency in detail on military and strategic questions, state and position of military units, their equipment, and other questions, such as the need for the relocation of the Main Staff and highest authority organs to more suitable places." Can you comment, Mr. Brown, on these minutes and the other minutes that you have seen in respect of the communications?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think they are on face value somewhat self-evident in that or self-explanatory that the senior military leadership are briefing the Presidency, sometimes in -- in significant detail, and -- and that would seem to echo some of the comments from the army report in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we turn to tab 38, please, Mr. Brown. 38 is a 9 June 1992 report from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. It is sent to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina army Main Staff and to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency. So this document -- what is this document, Mr. Brown? Explain this to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: This document, which I do reference in the report, is a document -- in summary, there had been a meeting of the Autonomous Region of Krajina at which the issue of Muslims and Croats who were serving in the army, and in particular, I think, the 1st Krajina Corps, had come up at a -- at a meeting of the -- the ARK Crisis Staff. And there had been a -- an ultimatum issued that these Muslims and Croats, 67 I think are highlighted here, should be removed or they say they would take over control of the armed forces; "they" presumably meaning the local ARK leadership. This report comes from the 1st Krajina Corps, and it's signed by Colonel Milutin Vukelic, who is the assistant commander for morale; he was a staff officer under General Talic, the corps commander. And he's reporting to the Presidency and to the Main Staff about this meeting, and he says that the -- "We consider the demand is justified, but it's impossible to find adequate professional replacements." So although he agrees with the sentiment, there is some implication if 67 officers are presumably going to have to be removed from the 1st Krajina Corps. So he sends this document up on the 9th and asks for, you know, a solution to the -- to the problem. On the same day, I think this document, if I remember rightly, was sent sometime in the afternoon. Yes, I think it's sent in the afternoon. I believe on the same day, the Main Staff, Ratko Mladic, sent an order down sending all officers of non-Serb -- or Muslims and Croats, sent them to Belgrade, where their status would be resolved, and in essence that meant that Muslims and Croats who were in the 1st Krajina Corps were then removed. But it's of interest that this issue, which clearly was of some significance to the 1st Krajina Corps, is also sent to the Presidency, presumably signifying it's -- it's an important issue. And it also highlights that the corps had a capability of disseminating a report to the Presidency, again highlighting maybe the communication issue that we've talked about in the VRS Main Staff report that it was a functioning communications system. And in this case, the response from the Main Staff was very quick, and -- and I think it was on the very same day that the response was that these non-Serbs were to be sent to Belgrade and their status resolved. Again, indicating that not only was the communication up the chain quick but that the communication and the response back down the chain was pretty quick, as well, on issues of -- of some importance, presumably, to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we return to tab 37.1, Mr. Brown. And staying with the topic of keeping the political leadership of the Republika Srpska informed by the army itself, can you discuss this document, which is dated the 1st of June, which is entitled "A meeting of the corps commanders," and it is signed by the Chief of Staff, General -- Major General Milan Milovanovic. Can you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document which is sent to the corps from the Main Staff indicating that "Pursuant to a decision of the Presidency and the Main Staff of the army, a meeting of the political leadership of the republic and the military commanders was to be held in Pale on the 3rd of June." And this instruction orders -- this is an order actually -- orders that the corps commanders and the commanders of the Air Force and air defence were to attend that meeting and to prepare a briefing, which included a map indicating troop dispositions within the corps, state of affairs, composition, manpower, disposition, enemy intentions, proposals for further activities, and problems. So it's not only the current state but -- but the difficulties that the corps had and also suggestions for further activities. And each corps commander was to last -- was to give a briefing to that effect, and it goes to all the corps. This -- this document indicates that the briefing was to be on the 3rd of June. There's another Krajina Corps document, dated the 9th of June, which makes direct reference to a directive which the corps had received from the Main Staff and which they themselves were following or -- or carrying out. Now, I haven't seen that directive but they clearly had got a directive round about maybe the 8th, 7th or 8th, or maybe even on the 9th of June. And it is possible, and I only suggest here, that what you have is the Main Staff ordering the corps or the corps commanders to attend a briefing pursuant to a decision of the Presidency and the Main Staff, i.e., the senior political leadership, the senior military leadership, at which they themselves were to brief in some detail. And then a few days later there's a reference to a directive which came out, and that the 1st Krajina Corps followed that directive. And I know they followed the directive because we have General Talic's corps-wide instructions on the 9th and 10th of June. So it may well be a pattern that what there was a request to -- to the corps, a briefing in -- on the 3rd of June, and potentially what fell from that briefing was a directive a few days later, and what fell from that directive was combat operations that the corps conducted -- certainly the 1st Krajina Corps conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, can we turn to tab 40, please. Again, on the issue of meetings between the military and the political leadership. This is a document that is dated the 12th of September, 1992. It is to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Can you tell the Judges what this document is about, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a Sarajevo-Romanija Corps document disseminated, I believe, to the subordinate units of that corps, which highlights that there was a meeting that had happened on the 6th of September, 1992, in Jahorina, attended by the SRK command, brigade commanders, presidents of Municipal Assemblies, chief of municipal recruiting officers, members of the Main Staff, and members of the government and Presidency of the Serbian Republic. Now, I believe that this, although the SRK is not necessarily my area of expertise, I believe this came around the time that General Galic took control of the SRK. I think he -- he had arrived in or around that time period. So, clearly, the change of command of the SRK would have been some -- of some significance, and it may well have been that one of the reasons why this briefing had happened was because of this important change of command in the corps. But it makes reference to a meeting that happened in Jahorina on the 6th, and it discussed the issue of tasks. In essence, we received tasks from the conference, so we received tasks from the -- the conference on military and political matters with all those individuals. And General Galic outlines what those tasks are. And they're -- they're quite lengthy and quite detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown -- Mr. Brown, we won't go, I don't think, any further with this document unless there's another important feature you want to point out to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Maybe the only issue I would highlight reflects back to this issue of the strategic goals of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which by then was to maintain a blockade. And -- and the tasks are given, which seem to indicate, you know, they're to continue with decisive defence. So not necessarily going on a defensive position but they're holding the territory that they already had. Maybe that that could link back to this issue of the strategic goals and keeping the blockade maintained in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you know that the Judges are always a bit behind. Could I take the witness back to tab 35.1. At the end of that document, after the briefing by the Generals Mladic and Gvero, it reads, "All details were discussed, but they were not put on the record because of their level of confidentiality." Is that language you have found at other occasions, as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that language being used, Your Honour. I noticed it was also in the previous Presidency, where Mladic briefed, but the details were not put in into the minutes. It's -- it's not something that I remember in other -- in other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was the situation at that time such that information on what happened militarily was very sensitive -- I mean, I do understand that military operational information is always sensitive, but was there any reason to assume that it was specifically sensitive at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to make any projections on that, Your Honour. I'm not sure why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know, no problem. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of what the Judge -- Judge Orie, has just asked, I would refer you, Mr. Brown, to page 45, I believe of this army report, paragraph 2.1.1, which is the attitude of the international community to the resolution of the Yugoslav crisis and the war in the territory of the former BH. And it -- this paragraph says that the -- "The situation in the former Yugoslavia in the fullest expression of which was the civil ethnic religious war in the territory of the former BH was the focus of media attention and diplomatic and political activities," and it goes on. And then further down in the paragraph, that same paragraph, it says, "The Serbian people, who were subjected to inconceivable demonisation, the unscrupulous information and propaganda war in almost all of the powerful states of the world, in particular the orchestrated planting of lies about alleged massacres of civilians, the bombardment of civilian facilities, POW camps, ethnic cleansing, the raping of women, and other media fabrication served to project a distorted picture of the national interests of the Serbian people and the alleged indisputable responsibility of the Serbs for all the horrors of the war in the territory of the former BH. International public opinion was largely turned against the Serbs." Now, Mr. Brown, you stated in your report - I believe it is in paragraph 2.248, which is at 154 of your report - that the international press, "who appeared to be generally as anti-Serb and particularly singled out for criticism." Mr. Brown, was the army, based on your review of the documents, sensitive, in the period of August, September, and earlier, to the criticisms it was receiving by the international media?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. And -- and I would say in some documents it's not just that -- necessarily that time, but there is this undercurrent that -- that there was -- the international press were -- were misreporting. But in terms of August, in particular in relation to camps, I know of one document in particular from the Krajina Corps which they specifically point to the criticisms of the international press about the existence of what they call concentration camps and the negative impact that that is having. So yes, they were. And it's clear, I think, from the Krajina Corps, certainly, the documents there, that the military were acutely aware of -- of the media reporting and, in fact, established their own press centre. Well, in fact, the VRS established press centres throughout the area of responsibility, but the Krajina Corps had its press centre in which it was both providing information which they say could counter that and -- and presumably also making them aware of what the international media were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we turn your attention, Mr. Brown, to tab 41 on that very topic. Mr. Brown, this is a previous Prosecution exhibit, Prosecution 583, Trbojevic, tab 58. If I could direct your attention. This is a 6th August 1992 document from the 1st Krajina Corps command, Department of -- for Intelligence and Security Affairs, and it is signed by Chief Colonel Stevan Bogojevic, and it says "the 5th Corps Command," which obviously in August was no longer in existence, was it, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No. I'm assuming they were just required to keep the stamps and used the stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: To the security of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you comment on this document, and particularly the --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, this was -- yeah, this was the document I referred to. And they realised there were a lot of people in Manjaca that don't deserve to be there, don't deserve to be treated as prisoners of war, don't have weapons, didn't participate in combat, they were not in uniform, and in order to free up space, they're asking the Prijedor police to -- to, in essence, review these -- these prisoners. And it highlights at the end the -- "As you know, we have recently been attacked by the European world media in connection with the existence of concentration camps. So this is sufficient reason to carry out this selection." And I think this comes around the time that the issue of camps had arisen in the media in Prijedor, around that first week -- first week in April. So it seems to me that the security chief of the corps is aware that many people in Manjaca, which is a camp that the 1st Krajina Corps ran, didn't deserve to be treated as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, before we proceed, in view of the fact that there's been reading from the document, and to make the record clear, of course "concentration camp" appears in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It does. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the final analysis -- in your final analysis, Mr. Brown, in terms of what was available to the -- the VRS from the corps level to the Main Staff, the army in general, and to the political superiors, was there sufficient communication equipment and infrastructures to prevent them to receive information from outside in respect of what was happening in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a result of their actions?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I object to that question. It's quite clear that the report on which the witness was brought here to give evidence is one that's very specifically delineated to a particular area and a particular time frame and what have you. Now, as a result of the additional exhibit list this morning, we have a more broader scope of evidence being brought out from this witness, and the -- the question that's being asked there, Your Honour, I would submit the witness should not be allowed to answer on the basis of what he has already indicated are the limitations of the report he actually produced for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What limits exactly -- of course, the witness said some limitations he has drawn our attention to, but what exactly would here prevent him from having any knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the report is "Military developments in the Bosanska Krajina 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: This is a more broader question about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The documents that are being examined by this witness are specifically delineated in this report. The limitations of the report are specifically delineated in the report, as were circumscribed by the evidence he gave earlier today in his evidence in chief about the limitations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's broadening, Your Honour; I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, of course sometimes subjects are -- I mean, information you receive from -- for example, from foreign press or foreign -- could relate to military matters, as well. So let's ask the witness whether he thinks that the limitations he has mentioned at the beginning of his testimony are such that he has difficulties in answering the question, and perhaps he could also explain to us that if he thinks he can answer the question, how this related, both, to his subject and why it's not bothered by the limitations he expressed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I did highlight the limitations of the report, but I -- I have worked in that field for some time. I was within the military analysis team looking at military documentation between 1998 and last year. Many of the documents I use in the report also do -- or a number of documents do speak to the issue of communications. The combat analysis, readiness report of 1993 is a document I've looked over many times. And, you know, as best I can I think I can comment on -- on some of that material. Some of the documents that I have not included which I've commented on, I don't think are ones that are necessarily outside my -- my scope, and I believe I -- I can -- I can cover those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may give the comments you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question for me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, what I asked you is whether the communications structures and infrastructure in the Republika Srpska that was extant could permit and did permit the Main Staff -- VRS army members from the Main Staff, down to the corps level, and up to the Supreme Command and superior civilian command to be aware of the various serious criticisms that were being made against the Serbs in respect of their conduct in pursuing the war.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I think the communications structures were there. The communications structures worked; they themselves said the communications structures were very good. There are documents which seem to bear that out in the passage of information up and down the chain. The Presidency minutes would indicate that, at least in the one you've just shown me, that the international media issue was briefed and raised. The army themselves made note of concerns they had relating to the international media. And so I would say yes, they -- they were able to be made aware of this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's 7.00, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- I'm prepared to conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll finish for the day. I have one issue I'd just like briefly to address, but a very minor one, I would say. Ms. Loukas, the Chamber has asked questions in relation to the Celinac and Teslic dossiers and wanted to know who Milos was. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh yes, Your Honour, yes. I recall that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have considered that, and with this information, the Chamber accepts these parts of the dossiers, admits them into evidence. And as you know, one week after admission you always can comment on it because the dossiers, of course, are not discussed with witnesses. So on this issue, the decision of the Chamber is they are only now -- you remember, we had additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just reading it on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I might not be that clear at this moment. Usually the Chamber receives the documentation, the dossiers; we admit them into evidence, but we grant one week to the Defence to make further objections or observations.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I would indicate, just in relation to this -- this question of Milos. Your Honour will recall that I cross-examined a witness in relation to a document involving that particular individual, and it -- we left it as marked for identification. So at some point we'll have to tender that formally now that the identity of Milos has been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the other one was the Chamber has asked the Prosecution to clarify the relevance of tab 2 and the highlighted portions of tab 5 in the Novi Grad dossier. The OTP has now clarified that tab 2 was included to show the presence of the accused at a meeting, because someone says that Mr. Krajisnik was at a meeting; not the meeting reported on, but it's part of what is said during that meeting. And the second issue to be that in respect of tab 5, that only the highlighted portions of tab 5 were tendered. That means that it's limited to the first four pages because as far as I can see, only in the first four pages of tab 5 there appear any highlights. The Chamber with these limitations admits into evidence, Ms. Loukas, and, as usual, seven days for the Defence to make objections in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
